analysis.one_liner: Slashes the capital gains tax rate to 15 percent and adjusts investment costs for inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut the capital gains rate to 15 percent, backed by 19 senators, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cut the tax rate on long-term investment gains to 15 percent for individuals and corporations, with a 7.5 percent rate on the portion of gains falling within low- and middle-income tax brackets. It would also let investors raise the "cost basis" of stocks and business property to account for inflation since purchase, which shrinks the gain that is taxed. The bill contains no offsetting tax increases, so the lost revenue would add to deficits or shift the tax burden. It never received a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who sell stocks and business property at a profit — a group heavily concentrated among the wealthiest households — plus corporations holding appreciated assets, mutual funds, and real estate investment trusts. The 15 percent rate would cut the top capital gains tax roughly in half (from the 28 percent individual top rate and 34 percent corporate rate), and inflation indexing would further shrink taxable gains for anyone who held an asset for years. The special 7.5 percent rate for low- and middle-income taxpayers applies only to the slice of gains that fits within the 15 percent income bracket, so its dollar value for most working families would be small or zero, since most have little or no capital gains.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Stock and property investors, mostly wealthy

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the maximum tax rate on long-term capital gains to 15 percent for individuals, down from a top rate of 28 percent (the CRS summary describes the prior rate structure as 34 percent), with a 7.5 percent rate on gains falling within the low- and middle-income bracket range.
Cuts the corporate capital gains rate to 15 percent from 34 percent, so corporations selling appreciated assets pay far less.

Lets sellers of corporate stock and business property multiply their cost basis by an inflation ratio based on the GNP deflator, erasing inflation-driven paper gains from taxation; the adjustment passes through to shareholders of mutual funds, REITs, partnerships, and S corporations.
Reduces the alternative minimum tax rate applied to capital gains to 15 percent, so the AMT would no longer claw back most of the benefit of the lower rate.
Indexes the $3,000 annual limit on deducting capital losses for inflation, letting noncorporate investors deduct more in loss years.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The bill contains no offsetting revenue provisions, so the revenue lost from the lower rates and inflation indexing would be financed through larger deficits or through other taxes. Because capital gains are earned overwhelmingly by higher-income households, the tax cut's benefits would concentrate at the top while its fiscal cost would be spread across everyone who pays federal taxes or bears the burden of federal debt.
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers, through deficits or other taxes

drawbacks.text: The bill has no revenue offsets of any kind, so the rate cut and indexing would directly increase deficits or force other taxes to rise to pay for it.

The benefits would flow overwhelmingly to the small share of households that own most stocks and appreciated property; the 7.5 percent rate for low- and middle-income taxpayers applies only to gains fitting within the 15 percent income bracket, and most working families have little or no capital gains income at all.

The indexing provision applies only to capital assets like stock and business property, not to wages, giving investment income a tax advantage over income from work; a taxpayer could also owe tax on nominal gains while deducting losses only in inflation-adjusted terms, an asymmetry critics of indexing have long pointed out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward tax cut for holders of appreciated assets, and its design concentrates the benefit there: the rate cut and inflation indexing are worth the most to whoever holds the most stock and business property, while the low- and middle-income 7.5 percent rate covers such a narrow slice of gains that most families would see little from it. With no offsets, the entire cost would land on the deficit or on other taxpayers. Even on its own terms — encouraging venture capital — the benefit is speculative, while the revenue cost is certain.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the same day it was introduced and sat there until the Congress ended two years later, never reaching a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Kasten introduced the bill on March 13, 1991, joined by 16 original cosponsors including Senators Mack, Shelby, Helms, Lott, McCain, Hatch, Gramm, D'Amato, and Thurmond.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day; no further action of any kind was taken on it.
The Finance Committee never voted the bill out, and the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, killing the bill without any floor or committee vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Treasury and the general taxpayers who would otherwise have financed the tax cut are better off that it never advanced; investors seeking the 15 percent rate gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers who would have funded the cut

for.name: Sen. Robert W. Kasten Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 16 original cosponsors on the day of introduction.

for.name: Sen. Richard Shelby
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; he was the bill's only Democratic supporter among its 19 sponsors.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill after its introduction.

for.name: President George H.W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Had made a lower capital gains rate a signature administration tax proposal, pushing the idea that a rate cut would spur investment.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred on the day of introduction; never marked it up or reported it out.

against.name: Sen. Lloyd Bentsen
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the two years it sat in his committee.

sides.party_line_note: 18 of the bill's 19 sponsors were Republicans; the sole Democratic supporter was Senator Richard Shelby of Alabama, and no chamber vote ever tested broader support.

industries.note: The 15 percent rate plus inflation indexing would cut the tax on investment gains by more than half for high-bracket taxpayers. Because capital gains income is concentrated among the wealthiest households, the forgone revenue would be a transfer from general taxpayers to asset holders.

The bill is explicitly aimed at boosting venture capital by taxing gains on startup and business investments at 15 percent with inflation protection. Cheaper after-tax exits could attract more funding to young companies, but the benefit would come at the cost of lost federal revenue.

industries.industry: Mutual funds and real estate investment trusts
industries.note: The indexing rules are written to pass through to shareholders of regulated investment companies, REITs, and partnerships, so fund and trust investors would get the inflation adjustment automatically. The benefit flows to their shareholders, who skew toward higher incomes.
The corporate capital gains rate would drop from 34 percent to 15 percent. This lowers taxes on corporate asset sales without any offset, adding to the deficit that all taxpayers bear.
